verdict: OK to lend in Madurai tyres and rubber, but only to borrowers tied to the TVS Srichakra supply chain or to replacement/off-highway niches, structured on receivables and inventory with monthly stock statements; avoid small OEM-only compounders and job-workers with no pricing power.
title: Madurai Tyres & Rubber: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
Madurai's tyre cluster is anchored by TVS Srichakra's Vellaripatti plants, which run two-wheeler capacity of 210-235 lakh tyres a year at 80-85% utilisation and off-highway capacity of 75-85 metric tons a year at 75-80% utilisation [2][3]. Around that anchor sit compounders, tread-rubber and retread units, moulders and industrial rubber parts makers. **Cash is made on conversion margin and machine hours, not on brand; the anchor sets price and the small unit absorbs the swing.** Natural rubber and other inputs squeeze margins even as volumes hold [4], so a supplier's margin is a pass-through negotiation, not a pricing decision.

## Where value and cash sit
Value sits in the anchor's order book and in the replacement market, which is roughly 70% of overall volumes nationally [10]. Working capital sits in rubber inventory and in receivables from the anchor and tier-I buyers; capex is press-and-mould heavy with a long payback. **So when a proposal lands, check the receivable days against the anchor's payment cycle and the inventory days against rubber price movement; if inventory days are rising while sales are flat, ask whether the borrower is holding rubber as a price bet.** Peer evidence shows the strain: JK Tyre's interest cost rose 12% y-o-y with working capital facilities almost fully utilised and interest cover at 2.19x [8] - old FY19 data, but the pattern of full utilisation is what you underwrite against.

## What has changed now
National output for NIC 22 is up 21.4% y-o-y and 18.2% April-to-date [D], and bank credit is growing 21.0% against that 18.2% output, a gap of 2.8 pp [D] - **credit is running ahead of output, so some of the growth you will see in proposals is borrowed demand, not real demand.** Locally, TVS Srichakra has approved up to Rs 220 crore of capex, split Rs 110 crore each for two-wheeler and off-highway, with the off-highway 25% addition due in H1 FY28 and the two-wheeler 5% addition in H1 FY29 [2][3]. Peer results confirm the pattern of expansion into soft margins: JK Tyre is taking staggered price increases and expects double-digit revenue growth [6], and Himadri is pushing Birla Tyres toward OTR and OHT with exports [7]. **The growth is real but it is in off-highway and export-linked niches, not in plain two-wheeler volume.**

## Who to pursue and how to grow safely
Pursue suppliers and job-workers with a confirmed purchase order from the Vellaripatti expansion, off-highway and OTR component makers, and replacement-market distributors with diversified buyers [2][3][7]. Avoid single-buyer compounders, units with no order backing for new presses, and borrowers whose only collateral is a second-hand press. **Structure against the order: sanction against the PO, release in tranches on commissioning evidence, and take monthly stock and receivable statements plus the anchor's payment advice.** Covenant a debt-service cover and a receivable-days ceiling, and take the anchor's confirmation of dues every quarter.

## Early-warning signs
- Monthly stock statement (monthly): inventory days rising two months running -> freeze further drawing power and inspect godown.
- Receivable ageing from anchor (monthly): top-buyer dues past agreed cycle -> ask for the anchor's payment advice and reprice.
- Utilisation certificate (quarterly): capacity use falling below the plant's stated band [2][3] -> shift to need-based limits.
- Rubber price and margin note (quarterly): margin compression without a price pass-through [4][6] -> cut tenor and seek additional collateral.
- Credit growth vs output gap [D] (quarterly): gap widening -> tighten new-to-bank SME limits in the cluster.
